newsitem.title: FRANCE: Nothing EC can do about Renault closure-Van Miert.
newsitem.headline: Nothing EC can do about Renault closure-Van Miert.

text.p: European Competition Commissioner Karl van Miert said that, while he thought French carmaker Renault breached European Union directives when it closed a Belgian car plant, there was nothing the European Commission could do.
Van Miert made the comments in an interview to be published in Wednesday's edition of French financial daily Les Echos. A copy of the interview was released in advance.

Van Miert said that, if the directives had indeed been violated, the Belgian authorities and unions could apply to national courts in France and Belgium as the directives had been adopted in each country.
"But the European Commission, however, cannot tackle individual member states. I can only regret it," he was quoted as saying.
Van Miert said it appeared that Renault had breached the directive which says that, in the case of mass layoffs, workers representatives must be informed before and two alternatives discussed.
The second directive says that works committees must be informed of the company's strategy.
"In my opinion, Renault respected neither the spirit nor the letter of these two directives," Van Miert said.
He said an attempt in 1991 to give the EC powers to act in the case of layoffs that breached EU directives had never seen the light of day and to ask the EC to intervene now was not realistic.

Renault chairman Louis Schweitzer told reporters at the Geneva car show on Tuesday that the decision to close the Vilvoorde plant was "weighty and painful", but the move was necessary and the company preferred to tell the people affected the truth from the start.
"It seemed preferrable not to mask the reality from the start; not to enter into a game in which we would pretend to be negotiating when the outcome was known," Schweitzer said.
Schweitzer was not surprised by the outcry.
"It seems normal to me that a decision of this nature provoke a shock. If we had the feeling that the decision had not been necessary we would not have taken it," he added.
"It's a decision to concentrate industrial production going beyond the plant closure and that was not contingent on negotiation. There was no room for negotiation on the decision itself."
